Leicestershire
LES-tur-shur
n. (the midland county holding Lutterworth, where Wycliffe was rector and died in 1384 and whose bones were burned and cast into the Swift in 1428)
From Leicester, Old English Ligera ceaster, the Roman town of the Ligore people; with scir, a shire.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Leicestershire is the midland county of the Soar and the Wreake, and it holds the small town of Lutterworth in its southern corner. John Wycliffe was presented to the rectory of Lutterworth in 1374 and held it until he died there on the last day of 1384, having been driven out of Oxford and having spent his last years directing the translation of the Scriptures into English and writing against transubstantiation, the papal supremacy and the endowment of the church. He was struck down in his own church at the elevation of the host and died three days later. The Council of Constance condemned him in 1415 and ordered his remains dug up and burned; the sentence was carried out at Lutterworth in 1428 by Bishop Fleming, and the ashes were thrown into the river Swift, which runs into the Avon, the Avon into the Severn and the Severn into the sea. Thomas Fuller afterwards made the observation that the ashes were thus dispersed over the whole world, as his doctrine now is. The dictionary records the exhumation as the most futile act in English religious history.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to exhume as to dig out of the earth; to translate as to render into another language; to diminish as to lessen; to abide as to continue; and void as empty.

expand to see more

EXHUME, v.t. To dig out of the earth what has been buried; to disinter.

TRANSLATE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.

DIMINISH, v.t. To lessen; to make less or smaller by any means; to reduce; to take away a part.

ABIDE, v.i. To rest or dwell; to tarry or stay; to continue permanently or in the same state.

VOID, a. Empty; vacant; not occupied with any visible matter; having no legal or binding force.

Key Scripture

Rev 22:18 — "For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:"

Deu 4:2 — "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you."

Isa 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Modern Corruption

Midland county holding Lutterworth, where Wycliffe was rector from 1374 until his death in 1384 and where his bones were dug up and burned in 1428 and the ashes cast into the Swift.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the Council of Constance's sentence on a dead man, and the dictionary names it as the public confession of a church that had run out of arguments. Wycliffe had been answered in his lifetime only by deprivation and condemnation, never refuted; forty-four years after his burial a bishop was sent to dig him up, burn what was left and throw it in a river. That is not church discipline, which cannot reach the dead, and it is not theology. It is an attempt to unmake a thing already done, and Scripture's standing promise about the Word makes the attempt absurd in advance: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).

The second paragraph names the doctrine Wycliffe was condemned for holding and the dictionary holds with him, which is the sufficiency and finality of the written Word against additions. He argued that Scripture is the law of Christ and that what the church has added, the papal supremacy, the sacrifice of the mass, the mendicant orders, the whole apparatus of merit, is addition and must go. The rule he appealed to is given twice in Scripture at either end of the canon. Moses states it, “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2), and John closes the Revelation with the same guard, “If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book” (Rev 22:18). The effect of such a word once it is loose is not administrative, and the men at Lutterworth with their spades were handling something Jeremiah had described: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29). The Swift carried the ashes to the Avon and the Avon to the sea.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yasaph (H3254), to add; Hebrew reyqam (H7387), void; Hebrew patish (H6360), a hammer.

expand to see more

Hebrew yasaph (H3254) — to add, to increase, to do again; “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you”, Deuteronomy 4:2.

Hebrew gara' (H1639) — to diminish, to take away, to shave off; “neither shall ye diminish ought from it”, Deuteronomy 4:2.

Greek epitithemi (G2007) — to lay upon, to add to; “If any man shall add unto these things”, Revelation 22:18.

Hebrew reyqam (H7387) — emptily, in vain, void; “it shall not return unto me void”, Isaiah 55:11.

Hebrew patish (H6360) — a hammer, a forge hammer; “like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces”, Jeremiah 23:29.

Usage

"“Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you” (Deu 4:2) — the rule Wycliffe appealed to."

"“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — the exhumation of 1428 and its futility."

"“like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces” (Jer 23:29) — what the spades were sent against."
